messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I understand the worry about eroding trust, but I think when cities keep their local police tightly coupled with federal immigration enforcement, they end up scaring off residents who might otherwise report crimes or serve as witnesses. If someone fears a routine police contact could lead to deportation, they stop calling for help, and that leaves whole communities less safe, not more. In my view, local officers should focus on solving local crime rather than acting as an arm of federal immigration priorities they had no say in shaping. Limiting cooperation doesn't mean shielding wrongdoing, just keeping roles separate.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I hear that, and I agree community trust matters, but I think the bigger picture is that local jails often already have someone in custody, so a quick handoff to federal authorities seems safer than releasing them back onto the street. I worry that limiting cooperation can end up protecting people who genuinely threaten public safety, not just hardworking families trying to stay under the radar. Cooperation doesn't have to mean local police becoming immigration agents themselves, just not standing in the way of federal requests when someone is already flagged as a concern. I'd rather see practical coordination than a hard wall between agencies.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair point about safety, and I don't doubt some cases involve real risk, but I think there's a meaningful difference between everyday policing and turning local jails into a pipeline for federal enforcement regardless of the underlying offense. Losing that separation seems like it could deter victims and witnesses from ever approaching police, and immigrant communities themselves bear that risk too, since they're often the ones who most need to report crimes without fear. I'd also say the safety argument cuts both ways, since some residents feel less secure when they believe police involvement could upend their whole family over a minor matter. I don't think full cooperation is really a neutral choice either way.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I take your point that the risk doesn't fall on one side alone, and I won't pretend limiting cooperation carries zero cost. But I think the deeper issue is that dangerous people shouldn't simply be released back into neighborhoods when a safer alternative exists, and cities can't fully control what happens once someone reoffends after being let go. Federal agents still retain certain powers to act on their own within these jurisdictions regardless of local policy. [[CLAIM]]
